title: Exchanging self and other
hook: Shantideva: put yourself in another's place, completely

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lazy monk: Shantideva, thought to do nothing but eat and sleep, stood up and recited a masterpiece. Your line was the lazy one spoke. Whom did you surprise? Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

A stubbed toe. The hand goes straight down to it. Nobody tells the hand to do that, and the hand never stops to ask what the foot has done for it lately. It just goes, because the hand and the foot belong to one body. In the masterpiece the lazy monk recited, the guide to the bodhisattva's way of life, there's a chapter on meditation that takes that ordinary reflex and pushes it as far as it will go. What if the line around the body were drawn somewhere else? Today: exchange.
screen: `THE HAND GOES TO THE FOOT.` → `ONE BODY.` → `WHAT IF THE LINE MOVED?`

segments.voice: Shantideva builds it in steps. First, the sameness. I want to be happy and I don't want to suffer. So does everyone else, in exactly the same way. If that's true, he asks, what makes my pain the one worth guarding? Only habit. He uses the picture of the body: the hand protects the foot as a part of itself, and so, he says, beings can be cared for as parts of one life. Second, the exchange itself. Having seen that everyone is the same in wanting happiness, he turns it around. Put yourself where the other person stands, and look back. In one passage he has the practitioner take the place of someone worse off, then an equal, then someone better off, and look back at their old self from each seat, calling that old self he. From the other side of the table, my own pride looks very different. Third, why bother. Shantideva is blunt about it: the misery in the world comes from wanting happiness only for oneself, and the joy in the world comes from wishing others well. He calls this exchange a supreme secret, a practice for those who want to protect themselves and others quickly. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't erasing yourself, or pretending you have no needs. The practitioner still eats and sleeps. It's a shift of where the center sits, practiced on purpose, the way a musician practices scales. Tibetan teachers later built whole trainings on this chapter. In these verses his tone is plain and urgent, with nothing sentimental in it.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS THE SAME THING.` · `STAND THERE AND LOOK BACK.` · `A SUPREME SECRET.` · `NOT ERASING YOURSELF.` · then, large: `EXCHANGE SELF AND OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trade places for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you saw yesterday, anyone at all. Now sit where they sat. Feel their chair, their morning, their tiredness, what they were hoping for. From there, look across at yourself. What did they see? Don't judge it. Just look from their side for a while, then come home to your own breath. The bell holds the time.
Exchange. Shantideva's practice of standing where another stands and wanting their good as if it were your own, which he calls a supreme secret. Today's word.
Your line: exchange self and other. Today, choose one hour and spend it as someone else: in every small choice, ask what they would need. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 967 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP FOR THE PATH.`

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, exchanging self and other is taught from the eighth chapter of Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara, and it underlies mind-training practices in which practitioners imagine taking on others' suffering and giving away their own happiness.

original.note: Sanskrit for exchanging self and other: para, other; atma, self; parivartana, turning around.

notes: All Shantideva material paraphrased from Bodhicaryavatara ch. 8 (body/limbs image, sameness of wanting happiness, taking the place of a lower, equal and higher other and calling the old self 'he', the exchange as 'supreme secret', world's suffering from self-grasping). Confirm paraphrases and verse placement.
Sanskrit compound parātmaparivartana (BCA 8.120) and pronunciation; confirm spelling and stress.
'Tibetan teachers built whole trainings on this chapter' refers to lojong; stated without dates or names. Confirm.
Practice adapts the outline's 'spend one hour as someone else' to the two-minute sit, with the hour moved to the carry.
Audit: the three seats in BCA 8.140ff are lower, equal and higher, so the 'rival, envious, struggling' list was corrected; cut the unsupported 'more like a doctor than a poet' (the text is verse).
Editor: aligned the paraphrase of BCA 8.129 (misery from wanting one's own happiness, joy from wishing others happiness) instead of 'grasping at a self'.
